parole.significato: a suffix used to form instrument nouns
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech -dlo, from Proto-Slavic *-dlo, from Proto-Indo-European *-dʰlom.

parole.significato: a suffix usually indicating a mass noun derived from a verb, e.g. the stuff needed for or the product of some activity
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ivo.

parole.significato: forms masculine nouns, often referring to sounds
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-otъ.
Inherited from Old Czech -ovati, from Proto-Slavic *-ovati.

parole.significato: suffix appended to verbs to create a feminine noun, usually denoting an action
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech -tva, -tba, from Proto-Slavic *-tva, from Proto-Indo-European *-tweh₂.

parole.significato: suffix appended to words to create a feminine noun, usually denoting an action
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech -tva, -tba, from Proto-Slavic *-tva, from Proto-Indo-European *-tweh₂.
Inherited from Old Czech bez, from Proto-Slavic *bъzъ, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂ǵos.
Inherited from Old Czech bez, from Proto-Slavic *bez, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeǵʰs.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bъlbъ, from Proto-Indo-European *stl̥b-, an ablaut variant of *stelb (“post, pole, jamb”) (whence also stilbs, q.v.), from *stel- (“to put in a standing position, to erect; standing, immobile, stiff”) with an extra b. The semantic evolution was probably: “motionless, sti

parole.significato: wood consisting of pines, pine wood
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech bor, from Proto-Slavic *borъ. Because in Slovak and Polish dialects it means "marsh", it is sometimes associated with Proto-Slavic *bara, meaning the same. More probably it is connected with Proto-Indo-European *bʰor-u-. Compare also borůvka.

From bor + -oví. The noun bor comes from Proto-Slavic *borъ. Because in Slovak and Polish dialects it means "marsh", it is sometimes connected with Proto-Slavic *bara, meaning the same. More probably it is connected with Proto-Indo-European *bʰor-u-. Compare also borůvka.

From bor (“wood consisting of pines”) + -ový. The noun bor comes from Proto-Slavic *borъ. Because in Slovak and Polish dialects it means "marsh", it is sometimes being connected with Proto-Slavic *bara, meaning the same. More probably it is connected with Proto-Indo-European *bʰor-u-. Compare also b
Inherited from Old Czech bratr, from Proto-Slavic *bratrъ, *bratъ, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr. The archaic form bratří is ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic *bratrьja.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *brъzda (“bridle, horse bit”), further origin uncertain: perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrusdʰos, but a complicated Slavic etymology has also been proposed.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *borna.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *borna.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bukъ, apparently from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂ǵos (“beech tree”).
Inherited from Old Czech bieda, from Proto-Slavic *běda, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeydʰ- (“trust, be convinced”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *běda, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeydʰ- (“trust, be convinced”).
Inherited from Old Czech cěp, from Proto-Slavic *cěpъ, from Proto-Indo-European *skey-.
Inherited from Old Czech cpáti, from Proto-Slavic *cьpati/*stьpati, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *steyp- (“to be stiff, erect”). Compare stíbat. Cognate with Polish ćpać.
Inherited from Old Czech debř, from Proto-Slavic *dьbrь, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ- (“deep”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *diviti.
Inherited from Old Czech dlúhý, from Proto-Slavic *dьlgъ, from Proto-Indo-European *dl̥h₁gʰós. Compare Serbo-Croatian dug.

Inherited from Old Czech dno, from Proto-Slavic *dъno, *dъbno (“bottom”), which is probably from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewb-. Cognates include Lithuanian dùgnas (“bottom”), Latvian dubens (“bottom”), German Tief (“deep”) and English deep. Transposition from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewdʰ- to *dʰewbʰ- i

parole.significato: age (particular period of time in history)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech doba, from Proto-Slavic *doba (“time”) probably comes from Proto-Indo-European *dʰabʰ- (“appropriate”), which is also connected with Lithuanian dabà (“nature, character”) and dabar̃ (“now”), Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌳𐌰𐌱𐌰𐌽 (gadaban, “be appropriate”), so it is possible that originally it mea
From do- + brát (“to take”), which comes from Proto-Slavic *bъrati, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“carry”).
Inherited from Old Czech drobiti, from Proto-Slavic *drobiti, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrebʰ-.
Related to drobit, which comes from Proto-Slavic *drobiti, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrebʰ-. First attested in the 14th century.

parole.significato: disintegrated or crushed material, for example grit
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech drt (“crushed material”), from Proto-Slavic *dьrati, from Proto-Indo-European *der-. See also the verb drát.
Inherited from Old Czech duh, from Proto-Slavic *dǫ̀gъ. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewgʰ- (“to produce something useful, to be strong”).

Originally a past participle of dout (“to blow”), i.e. “blown”, meaning “empty inside”. Dout is Panslavic, probably merged from Proto-Slavic *dǫti (from Proto-Indo-European *dʰemH-) and Proto-Slavic *duti (from Proto-Indo-European *dʰew-).
Inherited from Old Czech déšč, from Proto-Slavic *dъždžь of uncertain origin, probably from Proto-Indo-European *dus-diu- (“bad day”), from *dus + *dyew-.
Inherited from Old Czech dřěvo, from Proto-Slavic *dervo, from Proto-Indo-European *dóru.
Inherited from Old Czech dřiemati, from Proto-Slavic *drě̄màti, from Proto-Indo-European *drēm-ye-ti, from *drem- (“to sleep”).
Inherited from Old Czech dóm, from Proto-Slavic *dȍmъ, from Proto-Indo-European *dṓm.
Inherited from Old Czech holý, from Proto-Slavic *golъ, from Proto-Indo-European *gelH- (“naked, bald”).
Inherited from Old Czech hovado, from Proto-Slavic *govędo, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷew-n̥d- < *gʷṓws. Compare говядо.
Inherited from Old Czech hovořiti, from Proto-Slavic *govoriti, from Proto-Indo-European *gow(H)- (“to call, cry”). Cognate with Serbo-Croatian govoriti.
Inherited from Old Czech hovězí, from Proto-Slavic *govęďь, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷew-n̥d- < *gʷṓws. By surface analysis, hovado + -í.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *gъrbъ (“hump”).
Inherited from Old Czech hrnúti, from Proto-Slavic *gъrtnǫti, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ger- (“to gather, collect”), similar to *gromada (“pile, heap”).

parole.significato: human palm bent into a form of a bowl or grasping something
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech hrst, from Proto-Slavic *gъrstь, from Proto-Slavic *gъr-t-, from Proto-Slavic *gъrtati, which comes from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ger- (“to gather”). Cognate with Old Church Slavonic гръсть (grŭstĭ), Serbo-Croatian gȓst, Russian горсть (gorstʹ), Polish garść and Slovak hrsť (“
Inherited from Old Czech jablon, from Proto-Slavic *ablonь, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ebol-ni-.

Inherited from Old Czech jaro, from Proto-Slavic *jaro, from Proto-Indo-European *yóh₁r̥ (“year, spring”). Cognate with English year, German Jahr (“year”), Latin hōra (“hour, time, season”), Ancient Greek ὥρα (hṓra, “year, season”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *àsenь.
Inherited from Old Czech jeden, from Proto-Slavic *edinъ, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos (“one, single”).
Inherited from Old Czech jěhně, from Proto-Slavic *agnę, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂egʷn-, the stem of *h₂egʷnós.

Inherited from Old Czech jelen, from Proto-Slavic *(j)elenь, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁el-en-i-, which is often being connected with *h₁el- (“yellow-brown”). Its Slavic cognates are Polish jeleń (“deer”) or Russian оле́нь (olénʹ, “deer”), other Indo-European cognates are Lithuanian élnis or álnis
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *esenь, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁es-en-, whence English earn and German Ernte (“harvest”).

parole.significato: kindergarten-like institution for very young children, between ages 0 and 3
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jasli, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ed- (“to eat”).

parole.significato: yoke (bar or frame of wood by which two oxen are joined)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech jho, from Proto-Slavic *jьgo, from Proto-Indo-European *yugóm.
Inherited from Old Czech jmě, from Proto-Slavic *jьmę, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥.
Inherited from Old Czech játry, from Proto-Slavic *ętro, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁entrom.
Inherited from Old Czech kapratie, a dissimilation of papraď, from Proto-Slavic *paportь, from Proto-Indo-European *parǝt-. Compare Polish paproć, Slovak papraď.

parole.significato: to breastfeed, to suckle, to nurse
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kojiti.
Inherited from Old Czech kolčava. Further origin uncertain; possibly cognate with klát (“to strike, stab, spike”) from Proto-Slavic *kolti, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₂-.
Inherited from Old Czech kopati, from Proto-Slavic *kopati, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kep-.
Inherited from Old Czech kopyto, from Proto-Slavic *kopyto, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱoph₂ós. Compare Serbo-Croatian копито.

Inherited from Old Czech kostřec, from Proto-Slavic *kostrьcь which is from Proto-Slavic *kostra (“skeleton”). This probably comes from several intermingling sources: from Proto-Slavic *kostr-, *kostь (“bone”) and at the same time the root *kes-, which is from Proto-Indo-European *kes- (“to scratch”
Inherited from Old Czech krk, from Proto-Slavic *kъrkъ, originally from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn, bend”).
From the plural form of kroupa, from Proto-Slavic *krupa, from Proto-Indo-European *kroupeh₂.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kortъ, closely related to *kortъkъ (krátký (“short”)); derived from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”). The original meaning was „something which was cut off“, shared with the synonymous *razъ (today ráz, compare Polish razy (“multiplied by, times”)). The origins mi
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъrčiti.
From earlier kčicě, inherited from Proto-Slavic *kočica, which is a derivative of *koka, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kewk- (“height, elevation”).
Inherited from Old Czech labut, labud, from Proto-Slavic *olbǫdь.
Inherited from Old Czech lado, from Proto-Slavic *lędo, from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ-, cognate with English land.
Inherited from Old Czech lehký, from Proto-Slavic *lьgъkъ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lengʷʰ-.

parole.significato: flax (any plant of the genus Linum)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech len, from Proto-Slavic *lьnъ from Proto-Indo-European *lino-.
Inherited from Old Czech lepiti, from Proto-Slavic *lěpiti, from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“to stick”). By surface analysis, lpět + -it (“causative suffix”).
Inherited from Old Czech levý, from Proto-Slavic *lěvъ, from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂- (“to be hidden”).

Inherited from Old Czech loni, lóni, from Proto-Slavic *olni, from Proto-Indo-European *ol-nei. Cognate with Polish łoni, Slovak vlani, Slovene láni, Serbo-Croatian lȃni/ла̑ни, Russian лони́ (loní), and Latin ōlim (“once”).

parole.significato: love (intense feeling of affection and care toward another person)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech láska, from Proto-Slavic *laska, *laskati, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂s-.
Inherited from Old Czech mdlý, from Proto-Slavic *mъdьlь of uncertain origin, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂w- (“weak, dim”). First attested in the 14th century.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mьňьjь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *meďi, locative singular of *meďa, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos. Cognate with Polish między and miedzy, Slovak medzi.
Inherited from Old Czech mlha, mhla, from Proto-Slavic *mьgla, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃migʰleh₂ (“mist, cloud”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mъlva.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *morъ, from Proto-Indo-European *mer-.

parole.significato: to stain (to coat a wooden surface with a stain)
parole.testo: Related to Proto-Slavic *marati (“to dirty”), from Proto-Indo-European *mer-/*mor- (“to blacken, to dirty; dirt spot”). Compare mourovatý.
Inherited from Old Czech nrav, from Proto-Slavic *nȏrvъ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂nḗr.
Inherited from Old Czech mravenec, from Proto-Slavic *morvъ, from Proto-Indo-European *morwi-.
Inherited from Old Czech mrtvý, from Proto-Slavic *mьrtvъ, from Proto-Indo-European *mr̥twós, *mr̥tós, ultimately from the root *mr̥-, *mer- (“to die”).
Inherited from Old Czech my, from Proto-Slavic *my, from Proto-Indo-European *wéy.
Inherited from Old Czech jmieti, from Proto-Slavic *jьměti.
Inherited from Old Czech měsiec, from Proto-Slavic *měsęcь, from Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁n̥s.
Inherited from Old Czech nehet, nohet, from Proto-Slavic *nogъtь, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃nogʰ-.
Inherited from Old Czech netopýř, from Proto-Slavic *netopyřь, from Proto-Indo-European *nekʷto-peryo.
Inherited from Old Czech nízký, from Proto-Slavic *nizъkъ, from Proto-Indo-European *ni-.
From Proto-Slavic *o(b), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ebʰi.

parole.significato: a prefix with various functions, e.g. expressing
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech ob-, from Proto-Slavic *ob, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ebʰi. See o.

Inherited from Old Czech obrat, from Proto-Slavic *obortъ. The stem of the expression comes from Proto-Slavic *vortiti, which is a causative to *vъrtěti (see Czech vrtět), which referred to something turning. This comes from Proto-Indo-European *wert- (“turn, rotate”).

parole.significato: pick (to remove from surface, e.g. fruit from a tree, meat from the bones)
parole.testo: From ob- + brát, from Proto-Slavic *bьrati, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“carry”).
Inherited from Old Czech ot, from Proto-Slavic *otъ, from Proto-Indo-European *éti.

From od- + mykat. The verb mykat comes from Proto-Slavic *mъknǫti (“to rush, move quickly”) (compare Polish mknąć), which is from Proto-Indo-European *(s)mewk-, *mewk- (“to make a quick movement, to slide”).

Deverbal from odpařit (“to vaporize”), from the noun pára (“vapour”), which is from Proto-Slavic *para, *parъ, derived from *pariti (“to steam, to burn”). Probably comes from Proto-Indo-European *preh₁-.
Inherited from Old Czech on, from Proto-Slavic *onъ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énos.

parole.significato: they (third person personal masculine animate plural)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech oni, from Proto-Slavic *oni, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énos.
Inherited from Old Czech orati, from Proto-Slavic *orati, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂erh₃-.

Derived from Czech verb orat (“to plough”), which is derived from Proto-Slavic *orati, + -ba. This is related to Lithuanian árti, Gothic 𐌰𐍂𐌾𐌰𐌽 (arjan), Middle High German erran, Latin arāre (all of them meaning "to plough"), Old Irish airim (“I plough”), Ancient Greek ἀρόω (aróō, “to plough”), Armen
Inherited from Old Czech osm, from Proto-Slavic *osmь, from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *pьkъlъ, from Proto-Indo-European *pik- (“pitch”). Cognate with Polish piekło.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *pero.

parole.significato: Agaricus (genus of fungi in the family Agaricaceae), including champignon
parole.testo: The word was introduced into biology in the sense of champignon by botanist Jan Svatopluk Presl in 1846, but existed already in Old Czech in the sense false hellebore (Veratrum) or "a plant, the roots of which can be roasted". Comes from Proto-Slavic *pekti (“bake”), which comes from Proto-Indo-Euro

parole.significato: plundering, looting (act of stealing or confiscating assets by an army from unarmed enemy citizens in time of war)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech plen, from Proto-Slavic *pelnъ, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“to earn, to sell”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *plěna, *pelena (“thin skin, thin fabric”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“skin”).

parole.significato: montane glacial lake, particularly in the Tatra Mountains
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *pleso, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pleth₂- (“wide, flat”).
Inherited from Old Czech pľvati, pľváti, plivati, from Proto-Slavic *pľьvati, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ptyēw- (“to spit, vomit”).
Inherited from Old Czech pláti, from Proto-Slavic *polti, derived from Proto-Indo-European *pol (“to burn, be warm”).
Inherited from Old Czech prach, from Proto-Slavic *porxъ, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pers-.
Inherited from Old Czech prděti, from Proto-Slavic *pьrděti, from Proto-Indo-European *perd-.
Inherited from Old Czech protiv, from Proto-Slavic *protivъ.
Inherited from Old Czech prst, from Proto-Slavic *pьrstь, originally from Proto-Indo-European *pers- (“rain, dust”).
Inherited from Old Czech pásti (“guard, nourish”), from Proto-Slavic *pasti, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂-s-, from *peh₂-.
Inherited from Old Czech pět, from Proto-Slavic *pętь, from Proto-Indo-European *pénkʷe.
Inherited from Old Czech přietel, from Proto-Slavic *prijateľь, from Proto-Indo-European *preyH- (“dear”). By surface analysis, přát + -tel.
From Proto-Slavic *podъ, from Proto-Indo-European *pṓds; cognate with Slovak pôda.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orbъ (“servant, slave”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃erbʰ- (“orphan, child slave or servant”). Compare English robot and Serbo-Croatian rob.
Inherited from Old Czech robiti, from Proto-Slavic *orbiti, from *orbъ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃erbʰ-.
Inherited from Old Czech robě, from Proto-Slavic *orbę, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃erbʰ- (“orphan, child slave or servant”).
From rob + -ův. Noun rob comes from Proto-Slavic *orbъ (“servant, slave”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃erbʰ- (“orphan, child slave or servant”).
From roj + -ník. The noun roj comes from Proto-Slavic *rojь (originally probably “current”), which comes from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reyH- (“to flow”). See also zdroj, řeka, řinout, ráj.
From Old Czech rosa, from Proto-Slavic *rosà, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rṓs.
From rváč + -ek. From the verb rvát se (“scuffle”), which is from Proto-Slavic *rъvati (“tear”), from Proto-Indo-European *Hrew- (“tear, dig”).

parole.significato: pure (free of foreign material or pollutants)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ryďь, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rūdʰ-yo-.
Inherited from Old Czech rósti, from Proto-Slavic *orsti, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃er-.
Inherited from Old Czech sazě, from Proto-Slavic *saďa (“something deposited”) ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sed- (“to sit”).
Inherited from Old Czech sedm, from Proto-Slavic *sedmь, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥.
Inherited from Old Czech slunce, from Proto-Slavic *sъlnьce, from Proto-Indo-European *sóh₂wl̥.
Inherited from Old Czech sláma, from Proto-Slavic *solma, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱolh₂mos.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *smykati.
Inherited from Old Czech snieh, from Proto-Slavic *sněgъ, from Proto-Indo-European *snóygʷʰos.

Inherited from Old Czech smědý (where m changed into n probably because of the resemblance with hnědý (“brown”)), from Proto-Slavic *smědъ, whose origin is ambiguous. It might come from Proto-Indo-European *směh₁- (“to dirty”).

parole.significato: to sleep (to rest in a state of reduced consciousness)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech spáti, from Proto-Slavic *sъpati, from Proto-Indo-European *swep-.
Inherited from Old Czech stúpiti, from Proto-Slavic *stǫpiti, from Proto-Indo-European *stab- (“to support”). Compare Upper Sorbian stupić, Polish stąpić, Serbo-Croatian stupiti.

Originally “what towers above” (see also strmý, strměti). Inherited from Old Czech strom (“tree; mast”), from Proto-Slavic *stromъ, from *strьmъ, probably from Proto-Indo-European *ter-, *ster- (“hard”).
Inherited from Old Czech státi, from Proto-Slavic *stojati, from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂-.
Inherited from Old Czech státi, from Proto-Slavic *stati, from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂-.

parole.significato: projectile (to be fired from a weapon)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech střěla, from Proto-Slavic *strěla, from Proto-Indo-European *strel-, *strēl-, from *ster- (“line, streak, stripe; jet, spurt; beam”).
Inherited from Old Czech svatba, from Proto-Slavic *svatьba, from *svatъ (“kin”), from Proto-Indo-European *swe-.
Inherited from Old Czech svině, from Proto-Slavic *svinьja, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *suH-.

parole.significato: one's own; belonging to the subject, of the subject, or related to the subject; reflexive possessive pronoun; thus rend…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech svój, from Proto-Slavic *svojь, from Proto-Indo-European *swoyos, from Proto-Indo-European *swé.
From Old Czech sieci, from Proto-Slavic *sěťi, from Proto-Indo-European *sek- (“to cut”).
Inherited from Old Czech sieci, from Proto-Slavic *sěťi, from Proto-Indo-European *sek- (“to cut”).

parole.significato: salt (A common substance, chemically consisting mainly of sodium chloride (NaCl), used extensively as a condiment and p…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech sól, from Proto-Slavic *solь, from Proto-Indo-European *sḗh₂l.
Inherited from Old Czech tenký, from Proto-Slavic *tьnъkъ, from Proto-Indo-European *ténh₂us.
Inherited from Old Czech trak, from Proto-Slavic *torkъ.
Inherited from Old Czech táhnúti, from Proto-Slavic *tęgnǫti, from Proto-Indo-European *tengʰ- (“to pull”). Doublet of tíhnout.

parole.significato: to ask, to inquire, to enquire
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tędzati, from Proto-Indo-European *tengʰ- (“to pull, to burden”).
From tři, from Proto-Slavic *trьje, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes.
Inherited from Old Czech umřieti, from Proto-Slavic *umerti, from Proto-Indo-European *mer-. By surface analysis, u- + mřít.

parole.significato: to fall asleep (to pass into sleep)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech usnúti, from Proto-Slavic *usъnǫti (“to fall asleep”), from *u- (“away”) + *sъpati (“to sleep”), from Proto-Indo-European *swep-.
Inherited from Old Czech v, ve, from Proto-Slavic *vъ(n), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁n̥.
Inherited from Old Czech výmě, from Proto-Slavic *vymę, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ówHdʰr̥.
Inherited from Old Czech veš, from Proto-Slavic *vъšь, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *lewH-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *olni, from Proto-Indo-European *ol-nei. Cognate with Slovak vlani, Slovene láni, Serbo-Croatian lȃni/ла̑ни, Russian лони́ (loní), and Latin ōlim (“once”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *osa, from Proto-Indo-European *wobʰseh₂.

From the same source as vrtět (“to shake, wriggle, writhe”), Proto-Slavic *vьrtěti. Rejzek prefers a comparison with Latin forō (“to bore”) and borec (“to fight”) (both eventually from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH- (“to pierce”)).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *vor(p)ska, a derivation from *vorpa, from Proto-Indo-European *werp-, *werb- (“to turn, twist, bend”), see also Ancient Greek ῥέπω (rhépō, “weight”), Lithuanian varpas (“bell”).
Inherited from Old Czech vy, from Proto-Slavic *vy, from Proto-Indo-European *yúHs.
Inherited from Old Czech vábiti, from Proto-Slavic *vabiti (“to lure”), from Proto-Indo-European *wōb- (> Proto-Balto-Slavic *wōˀb-) or *weh₂b- / *weh₃b-.
Inherited from Old Czech vápno, from Proto-Slavic *vapьno, from *vapь (“dye”) (lime was originally used only as a dye). Maybe originated with Proto-Indo-European *wep-.
Inherited from Old Czech vieti, from Proto-Slavic *vějati, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂weh₁-.
Inherited from Old Czech viera, from Proto-Slavic *věra, from Proto-Indo-European *weh₁ros (“true”).

parole.significato: to delouse, to pick out lice
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech jískati, from Proto-Slavic *jьskati, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eys- (“to wish”). Compare Polish iskać.
Inherited from Old Czech vietr, from Proto-Slavic *větrъ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂weh₁-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *vysь (“height”).
Inherited from Old Czech věřiti, from Proto-Slavic *věriti, from Proto-Indo-European *weh₁ros ("true"). Cognate with Latin verus.
Inherited from Old Czech vóle, from Proto-Slavic *voľà, from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁- (“to want”).

From zadní + -ák (omitting the original prefix -ní). The adjective zadní (“back”) comes from Proto-Slavic *zadъ (“back part”), which seems to be derived from the preposition *za (“behind”) and Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“put”).

From za- + mykat. The verb mykat comes from Proto-Slavic *mъknǫti (“to rush, move quickly”) (compare Polish mknąć), which is from Proto-Indo-European *(s)mewk-, *mewk- (“to make a quick movement, to slide”).
Inherited from Old Czech zět, from Proto-Slavic *zętь, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁-.

parole.significato: to know (to be acquainted or familiar with)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech znáti, from Proto-Slavic *znati, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃-.
From Old Czech zob, from Proto-Slavic *zobь, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵebʰ- (“jaw, mouth”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zьrěti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zǫbrъ, *izǫbrъ, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *ǵómbʰos (“tooth, horn, peg”).
Inherited from Old Czech zváti, from Proto-Slavic *zъvati.
From z- + řítit, der Proto-Slavic *řutiti, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rew-. Cognates include Polish rzucić, Russian рушить (rušitʹ), Czech rýt or Latin ruo.
Inherited from Old Czech úhel, from Proto-Slavic *ǫgъlъ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂engulos (“joint?”), from *h₂eng- (“corner”).
Deverbal from utéct (“to flee, run away”). Equivalent to u- + těk, from Proto-Slavic *tekъ, from Proto-Indo-European *tekʷ- (“to run, flow”). Compare Polish ucieczka (“flight, escape”).
Inherited from Old Czech úzký, from Proto-Slavic *ǫzъkъ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enǵʰu-. Cognate with Latin angustus, Sanskrit अंहु (aṃhu).
Inherited from Old Czech čelo, from Proto-Slavic *čelo, from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₃os.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščirъ, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kei̯ro-. Cognate with dialectal Russian щи́рый (ščíryj), Belarusian шчыры (ščyry), Ukrainian щи́рий (ščýryj), Polish szczery, Slovak číry.
Inherited from Old Czech řúti, from Proto-Slavic *řuti, from onomatopoeic Proto-Indo-European *rew-.
Inherited from Old Czech šest, from Proto-Slavic *šestь, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs.

parole.significato: domino mask (a mask covering only the eyes and the space between them)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech kraboška, itself from Proto-Slavic *kȏrbъ (“basket”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerbʰ- (“to turn around, curve”). Cognate with Czech krabice (“box”) and Czech krabatý (“visibly distorted, unpleasant”). Ultimately cognate with Latin corbis (“basket”), German Kor

Inherited from Old Czech ščet, from Proto-Slavic *sъčetь, *ščetь, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱwek- (“to gape”). See also Sanskrit श्वञ्चते (śvañcate, “to become open”), उच्छ्वङ्क (ucchvaṅka, “cleaving open, gaping”). First attested in the 19th century.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *želěti.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žьlvъ, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰel-. Cognate with Upper Sorbian žołwja, Lower Sorbian žołw, Polish żółw, Serbo-Croatian žȇlvā and Slovene žélva. First attested in the 19th century.

Inherited from Old Czech život, from Proto-Slavic *životъ (compare Old Church Slavonic животъ (životŭ), Russian живот (život), Serbo-Croatian život), probably from a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wo-teh₂ (compare Lithuanian gyvatà (“life”), Sanskrit जीवित (jīvitá), Avestan 𐬔𐬀𐬌𐬌𐬊 (gaiio, “l

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *župa, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gewp- (“cavity, pit”). Compare Albanian gop (“cunt”), Polish żupa (“mine”), Proto-Germanic *kubô (“shed, hut”) and Ancient Greek γύπη (gúpē, “cave”). First attested in the 19th century.
